 # Connect 4: Power-Up Edition

An advanced connect four strategy game developed in C programming language that is more complex than the conventional version of connect four in terms of features and customization options.

---

## Table of Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Key Components](#key-components)
- [Technical Architecture](#technical-architecture)
- [Getting Started](#getting-started)
  - [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
  - [Compilation](#compilation)
  - [Download Pre-compiled Binaries](#download-pre-compiled-binaries)

---

## Overview

The regular Connect 4 game has certain restrictions, such as being confined to 6x7 squares, using two players only from one place, and having no record keeping features. The game **Connect 4: Power-Up Edition** overcomes these problems by providing a menu-based modular C program that allows variable board size and incorporates power-ups for players.

---

## Key Components

### Game Modes
- **Player vs. Player (PvP):** Two-player local mode with customizable names and unique disc icons.
- **Player vs. Computer (PvC):** Single-player mode with two AI difficulty levels:
  - **Easy:** Randomly selects valid columns.
  - **Medium:** Analyzes the board in order to make immediate moves leading to a win or preventing opponent from winning.

### Customization & Rules
- **Dynamic Grid Settings:** Configure grid sizes (such as 8x9, 10x10) and select number of discs for winning sequence (4 or 5 discs).
- **Power-Ups:** Unique discs to use once per game:
  - **Bomb Disc:** Removes surrounding discs when placed.
  - **Anvil Disc:** Removes an entire column when placed.
- **Undo Feature:** Undo last move during gameplay session.

### Saving & Progression
- **Scoring & Best Streaks:** Points scored depend on board size, effectiveness of moves and difficulty of AI. Saves both best and all time win streaks.
- **Saving & Loading Games:** Ability to serialize current game and continue playing later sessions.
- **Leaderboard & History:** Save statistics on persistent storage including total wins, losses, scores, and best streaks.

---

## Technical Architecture

The program employs the standard C libraries such as stdio.h, string.h, time.h, and stdlib.h and exhibits several concepts of system programming:

| Concept | Implementation |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Dynamic Memory Allocation** | Dynamically creates two-dimensional array boards based on user-defined numbers of rows and columns. |
| **Recursion** | Line counting function scans rows, columns, and diagonals dynamically regardless of board size and win length. |
| **Structure and Pointers** | Bundles player information, match status, and moves performed. |
| **File Handling** | Performs data handling for saved matches, match logs, and game ranking. |
| **Input Validations** | Validates menu input and column input to avoid out-of-bound actions. |

---

## Getting Started

### Prerequisites

- **Operating System:** Windows, Linux, or macOS
- **Compiler:** GCC (MinGW on Windows, GCC on Linux, or Clang / Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS)
- **IDE (Optional):** Visual Studio Code or Dev-C++

### Compilation

First, clone the repository and navigate into the project folder:

```bash
git clone [https://github.com/Asher-1971/Connect4](https://github.com/Asher-1971/Connect4)
cd Connect4
```

Then compile and run based on your operating system:

| Operating System | Compile Command | Run Command |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Windows** | `gcc main.c -o connect4.exe` | `connect4.exe` |
| **Linux** | `gcc main.c -o connect4` | `./connect4` |
| **macOS** | `clang main.c -o connect4` (or `gcc main.c -o connect4`) | `./connect4` |

### Download Pre-compiled Binaries

In case you do not want to compile the source code yourself, pre-compiled binaries are available for Windows, Linux, and macOS in the [Releases](https://github.com/Asher-1971/Connect4/releases) section.

| Operating System | File | Instructions |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Windows** | `connect4-windows-x64.exe` | Just download and double-click to execute, or execute from Command Prompt. |
| **Linux** | `connect4-linux-x64` | Run `chmod +x connect4-linux-x64 && ./connect4-linux-x64`. |
| **macOS** | `connect4-macos-universal` | Run `chmod +x connect4-macos-universal && ./connect4-macos-universal`. |

  - **Anvil Disc:** Removes an entire column when placed.
- **Undo Feature:** Undo last move during gameplay session.

### Saving & Progression
- **Scoring & Best Streaks:** Points scored depend on board size, effectiveness of moves and difficulty of AI. Saves both best and all time win streaks.

The program employs the standard C libraries such as stdio.h, string.h, time.h, and stdlib.h and exhibits several concepts of system programming:

| Concept | Implementation |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Dynamic Memory Allocation** | Dynamically creates two-dimensional array boards based on user-defined numbers of rows and columns. |
| **Recursion** | Line counting function scans rows, columns, and diagonals dynamically regardless of board size and win length. |
| **Structure and Pointers** | Bundles player information, match status, and moves performed. |
| **File Handling** | Performs data handling for saved matches, match logs, and game ranking. |
| **Input Validations** | Validates menu input and column input to avoid out-of-bound actions. |

Your AI currently searches the same board positions repeatedly through different move orders. A transposition table caches:

- Best move

- Negamax

- Iterative deepening
- Center-first move ordering
- Time budgets

- Normal AI searches deeper within 100 ms.
- Hard AI searches significantly deeper within 1000 ms.
- Fewer repeated calculations.
- Stronger tactical decisions.
- Faster response on larger boards.

2. Better move ordering using the cached best move
3. Immediate win/block checks before full search
4. Difficulty-specific evaluation/search settings

response.value:
A transposition table can support power-ups cleanly, but the **entire game state must be part of the cache key**.

Your current [`AIGameState`](/workspaces/Connect4/module3.h) already contains the important power-up fields:

```c
bool bomb_used[3];
bool anvil_used[3];
```

The hash must include:

- Every board cell
- Board dimensions
- Win length
- Current player
- Bomb-used status for Player 1 and Player 2
- Anvil-used status for Player 1 and Player 2
- Any future rule/configuration flags

A good design is a Zobrist hash:

```c
uint64_t hash_state(const AIGameState *state);
```

Each board piece and power-up flag receives a random key. The state hash is the XOR of all relevant keys.

### Transposition entry

```c
typedef struct {
    uint64_t hash;
    int depth;
    int score;
    int alpha;
    int beta;
    Move best_move;
    BoundType bound;
} TTEntry;
```

The cached `best_move` must include its type:

```c
typedef struct {
    int col;
    MoveType type;  // NORMAL, BOMB, or ANVIL
} Move;
```

That matters because:

```text
column 3 + normal move
```

is different from:

```text
column 3 + bomb move
```

### Example

These two states must produce different hashes:

```text
Same board
Same player
Same dimensions
```

but:

```text
State A: Player 1 has not used the bomb
State B: Player 1 already used the bomb
```

Otherwise, the AI could incorrectly reuse a result where a bomb move was legal when it is no longer legal.

### Power-up-specific concerns

#### Bombs

Bombs change several cells and then apply gravity. The resulting board must be hashed normally after the move. The cache does not need special bomb logic beyond including the updated board and `bomb_used` flags.

#### Anvils

Anvils remove a full column. Again, hash the resulting board and the updated `anvil_used` flag.

#### Move generation

The transposition table should store the full best move:

```c
best_move.col
best_move.type
```

Do not cache only the column.

#### Frontend bridge

When power-ups are enabled, [`getBestMove()`](/workspaces/Connect4/module3.h:78) must copy the frontend’s bomb/anvil usage state into `AIGameState`. Currently the bridge only copies the board, player, and move count.

### Important rule

The hash must also distinguish different rule configurations:

```text
Connect-4 vs Connect-5
6x7 board vs 10x10 board
Power-ups disabled vs enabled
```

Otherwise, cached results from one game configuration could contaminate another.

### Recommended architecture

```text
AIGameState
    ↓
Zobrist hash
    ↓
Transposition table lookup
    ↓
Negamax search
    ↓
Cache score, bound, and Move
```

So the transposition table is compatible with future power-ups. The key requirement is that it must cache the **complete state**, not just the board layout.

response.value:
## Main architectural limitations

### 1. Two different game-state models

Your frontend uses [`GameState`](/workspaces/Connect4/header.h):

- `char` cells: `'.'`, `'X'`, `'O'`
- Top-down board orientation
- `boardColsFilled`
- UI fields mixed into game state

Your AI uses [`AIGameState`](/workspaces/Connect4/module3.h):

- Numeric cells: `0`, `1`, `2`
- Bottom-up board orientation
- Search metadata
- Power-up flags

This creates conversion overhead and risks inconsistencies.

The bridge in [`getBestMove()`](/workspaces/Connect4/module3.h:78) currently converts the frontend state into an AI state, but it does not fully support future power-up state.

### 2. Power-ups conflict with current move counting

Your AI validator currently expects:

```text
number of pieces == move_count
```

That works for normal Connect 4.

It breaks when power-ups remove pieces:

```text
move_count = 10
board pieces = 7
```

A bomb or anvil can reduce the number of pieces while the move count still increases. Power-ups require separate concepts:

```c
int move_count;
int piece_count;
```

or move-count validation that allows removed pieces.

### 3. The bridge loses move type

`getBestMove()` returns only a column:

```c
int getBestMove(...)
```

But power-ups require more information:

```c
Move {
    int col;
    MoveType type;
}
```

The AI may choose:

```text
column 4 + bomb
```

but the frontend only receives:

```text
column 4
```

That means the power-up decision is lost.

You will eventually need something like:

```c
Move getBestMove(const GameState *frontend, ...);
```

or a separate result containing both column and move type.

### 4. Fixed-size arrays limit scalability

Both systems use fixed maximum dimensions:

```c
#define MAX_SIZE 20
#define MAX_DIM 20
```

This is safe and simple, but:

- Every AI state is copied as a large struct.
- Recursive negamax copies many large states.
- Larger boards become expensive.
- A transposition table consumes more memory.

For Connect 4-sized boards this is acceptable. For large custom boards, dynamic allocation or compact bitboards would eventually be better.

### 5. Copy-make search is expensive

Your AI uses:

```c
AIGameState next = *s;
```

for every move.

This is easy to reason about and safe, but it copies the entire board during search. With power-ups, copying is still correct, but bombs and anvils make each transition more expensive.

Possible future optimization:

```text
make move
search
undo move
```

However, copy-make is safer while the rules are still evolving.

### 6. Power-ups are compile-time controlled

Power-ups are currently controlled by:

```c
#define ENABLE_POWERUPS 0
```

That means enabling them requires recompiling the engine. A runtime rules configuration would integrate better:

```c
typedef struct {
    bool powerups_enabled;
    int win_length;
} GameRules;
```

Then the same executable could support:

- Normal Connect 4
- Connect 5
- Power-up mode
- Custom rules

### 7. UI and game logic are still coupled

[`game.c`](/workspaces/Connect4/game.c) currently handles:

- Menus
- Input
- Board display
- Difficulty selection
- Move execution
- Game-over messages

This works now, but makes future features harder:

- Save/load
- Undo
- Network play
- Replay
- Automated testing
- Multiple frontends

A cleaner architecture would separate:

```text
game.c       rules and state transitions
ai.c         negamax and transposition table
game_ui.c    menus and terminal display
save.c       persistence
```

## How well it integrates with the existing framework

### Transposition table: good integration

A transposition table fits naturally into [`module3.c`](/workspaces/Connect4/module3.c).

You already have:

- `AIGameState`
- `Move`
- `negamax`
- `find_best_move`
- Iterative deepening
- Move ordering

The main addition would be:

```text
hash state
lookup cache
reuse score if valid
store score and best move
```

This should not require major changes to the UI.

### Normal AI: very good integration

Normal mode already calls:

```c
getBestMove(game, game->winLength, 100);
```

The transposition table can be added entirely inside the AI engine.

### Hard AI: very good integration

Hard mode calls the same engine with a larger time budget. A transposition table should improve Hard more noticeably because it has more time to search.

### Easy AI: unaffected

Easy AI is random and does not use negamax, so the transposition table will not affect it.

### Power-ups: moderate integration effort

Power-ups are the area requiring the most architectural work.

Before adding them, I would change:

1. `getBestMove()` to return a full `Move`.
2. Frontend state to store power-up usage.
3. `valid_state()` so removed pieces are legal.
4. Save/load state definitions to include power-up flags.
5. The frontend move loop to apply `MOVE_NORMAL`, `MOVE_BOMB`, or `MOVE_ANVIL`.
6. The transposition hash to include power-up flags.
7. The UI to display and select power-ups.

## Overall assessment

Your current architecture is:

- **Good for a coursework-sized Connect 4 engine**
- **Safe and understandable**
- **Well suited to adding a transposition table**
- **Not yet ideal for power-ups or many future game modes**

The biggest architectural issue is not negamax. It is the duplication between frontend `GameState` and AI `AIGameState`.

The best long-term improvement would be to define one authoritative rules/state model, then let the UI and AI operate on that same model.

**Planning approach**

I need to plan without making any unnecessary changes. Since the user likely wants a broad outline, I can state the proposed architecture and simply ask for approval. There’s no need for a tool; inspecting the existing structure should be sufficient. I could recommend a modular layout, outline migration phases, and discuss interfaces. I’ll also mention the deferred transposition and clarify that there won’t be any implementation details included. Keeping it concise is key!

## Recommended target architecture

Do not implement the transposition table yet. First stabilize boundaries and state ownership.

```text
src/
  app/
    main.c
    app.c
  ui/
    terminal_ui.c
  game/
    game_state.c
    game_rules.c
    game_moves.c
    game_save.c
  ai/
    ai_api.h
    ai_search.c
    ai_eval.c
    ai_tt.c
  common/
    types.h
    hash.c
    random.c
```

For this repository, an initial migration could remain simpler:

```text
game.c      -> terminal menu and UI
start.c     -> board primitives and input
module3.c   -> AI engine
save.c      -> persistence
types.h     -> shared data structures
```

## Critical design decisions

### 1. Single authoritative state

Create one canonical `GameState` containing:

```c
typedef struct {
    int rows;
    int cols;
    int win_length;
    char board[MAX_DIM][MAX_DIM];

    int current_player;
    int move_count;
    int total_piece_count;

    bool bomb_used[2];
    bool anvil_used[2];

    Move last_move;
    bool game_over;
} GameState;
```

Remove the frontend AI split where possible. `char` and numeric board representations should not coexist.

The UI should translate only when necessary:

```text
User input
  -> Move
  -> applyMove(gameState, move)
  -> winner/game-over result
  -> render state
```

### 2. Unified move abstraction

Every action should use:

```c
typedef struct {
    MoveType type;
    int column;
} Move;
```

Move types:

```c
MOVE_NORMAL
MOVE_BOMB
MOVE_ANVIL
```

Power-ups become normal game transitions rather than special UI branches.

### 3. Pure rules module

`game_rules.c` should expose:

```c
bool isValidMove(const GameState *state, Move move);
MoveResult applyMove(GameState *state, Move move);
int checkWinner(const GameState *state);
bool isDraw(const GameState *state);
bool validateState(const GameState *state);
```

This module should not print text or read stdin.

Benefits:

- Frontend and AI use identical rules.
- Save/load validates through the same state validator.
- Power-ups use the same move pipeline.
- Unit tests become independent of terminal input.

### 4. Separate UI and gameplay loops

[`game.c`](/workspaces/Connect4/game.c) should become thin.

It should:

- Print menus.
- Collect menu choices.
- Call game initialization.
- Prompt for a move.
- Call `applyMove()`.
- Render board state.
- Report results.

It should not own win evaluation or legal-move implementation.

### 5. Stable AI API

Replace the bridge-dependent API with:

```c
typedef struct {
    Move move;
    bool found;
} AIMoveResult;

AIMoveResult getBestMove(
    const GameState *state,
    AILevel level,
    uint32_t time_budget_ms);
```

This should return both move type and column.

Use an internal AI state behind the API; copying the frontend state into a search state may remain for a short migration phase.

### 6. AI settings

Represent difficulty as configuration rather than an `if` chain:

```c
typedef struct {
    uint32_t time_budget_ms;
    int max_depth;
    bool iterative_deepening;
} AIConfig;
```

Levels:

```text
Easy    -> random legal move or shallow search
Normal  -> 100 ms tactical search
Hard    -> 1000 ms tactical search
```

Later, another module can add opening books or stronger evaluator weights.

### 7. Explicit move-count semantics

Track both:

```c
int move_count;
int piece_count;
```

`move_count` records attempts/transitions.

`piece_count` records pieces currently on the board.

This is required for future bombs and anvils because pieces can disappear.

### 8. Save/load module

Create `save.c/.h` with:

```c
bool saveGame(const char *path, const GameState *state);
bool loadGame(const char *path, GameState *state);
```

Save/load should:

- Validate the file header.
- Validate dimensions and win length.
- Validate every board cell.
- Validate move and piece counts.
- Validate turn parity.
- Validate power-up usage.
- Check gravity/column correctness.
- Reject already-terminal states if a game resume format requires ongoing play.

No UI code should know file formats.

### 9. Transposition table integration point

Introduce it only after the canonical state and move structures exist.

The cache key should include:

- Board
- Dimensions
- Win length
- Current player
- Move count
- Bomb/anvil usage
- Power-up configuration
- A complete move hash including `MoveType`

A transposition table should be internally owned by the AI:

```text
createAIEngine()
resetAIEngine()
getBestMove()
destroyAIEngine()
```

It should not be created or controlled by `game.c`.

## Migration phases

### Phase 1: Shared types

- Add `Move`, `MoveType`, and `GameRules`.
- Make [`GameState`](/workspaces/Connect4/header.h) authoritative.
- Remove duplicate AI/frontend state concepts.

### Phase 2: Extract rules

- Move win/tie logic out of UI modules.
- Move drop logic into `applyMove()`.
- Add state validation.
- Add pure unit tests.

### Phase 3: Extract UI

- Reduce [`game.c`](/workspaces/Connect4/game.c) to input/render orchestration.
- Keep AI difficulty configuration separate.

### Phase 4: Extract persistence

Keep a copy of an agent conversation, find earlier work, or share results with collaborators. Export or copy a conversation for a standalone record, or use session-history tracking and sync to search across your work.

VS Code maintains a searchable history of your Copilot harness sessions. Session sync (Experimental) can upload local session history to your GitHub account for cross-device access and sharing. With sync enabled, you can query work from VS Code, Copilot CLI, code review, and the GitHub Copilot app.

Synced sessions are private unless you explicitly share them. To resume a task rather than search its history, see [Find and resume a session](/docs/agents/run/sessions/manage-sessions#_find-and-resume-a-session).

## Export or copy a conversation

Exporting and copying create standalone records. These actions are separate from uploading session history with sync.

### Export a chat session as a JSON file

To save all prompts and responses from a conversation:

1.  Open the session in the Chat view.
2.  Run **Chat: Export Chat...** from the Command Palette (⇧⌘P (Windows, Linux Ctrl+Shift+P)).
3.  Choose where to save the JSON file.

### Copy chat messages as Markdown

Right-click a message or the chat background in the Chat view and choose:

*   **Copy**: Copy an individual prompt or response, including its text, thinking steps, and tool calls.
*   **Copy All**: Copy the entire conversation, including prompts, responses, thinking steps, and tool calls.
*   **Copy Final Response**: Copy only the final Markdown section after the last tool call, without intermediate steps.

 Important

Review exported files and copied messages before sharing. They can contain sensitive prompts, responses, or tool output.

## Enable or disable session sync (Experimental)

Check the [session sync status](#_session-sync-status) to see whether sync is enabled. Use chat.sessionSync.enabled Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders to set your preference:

*   To sync session history, set chat.sessionSync.enabled Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders to `true`. Local session tracking must also be enabled with github.copilot.chat.localIndex.enabled Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders .
*   To turn off session-history sync, set chat.sessionSync.enabled Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders to `false`. You can keep local session tracking enabled. Turning off sync does not delete data already synced to GitHub.com; see [Delete synced sessions](#_delete-synced-sessions).

Review [what gets tracked](#_what-gets-tracked) and the [privacy controls](#_privacy-and-data-control) before turning on sync. If your organization disables sync by policy, you cannot override that restriction.

 Note

Session-history sync is separate from the prompts and context sent to a model during an agent session. Turning off sync does not stop those model requests.

## Exclude repositories from sync

Use chat.sessionSync.excludeRepositories Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders to prevent sessions in specific repositories from syncing to the cloud. The setting accepts exact `owner/repo` names or glob patterns:

```
"chat.sessionSync.excludeRepositories": [
    "my-org/private-repo",
    "my-org/secret-*"
]
```

Sessions from matching repositories are not uploaded by session sync.

## Enterprise policy

For Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise users, two policies control session sync:

*   **GitHub.com enterprise policy** ("Store local sessions in the Cloud"): enterprise and organization owners configure this on GitHub.com to enable or disable cloud sync for their users.
*   **VS Code group policy** (`CopilotSessionSync`): when disabled, the chat.sessionSync.enabled Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders setting is forced to `false` and sessions stay local only.

 Important

Enabling the policy does not give administrators access to your session data. Synced sessions are tied to your personal account and are accessible only to you by default.

When disabled by policy, the session sync status shows **Disabled by policy** and users cannot override the setting.

## Share a session

Sessions are not shared by default. On GitHub.com, you can share a synced session for view-only access to anyone who has access to the repository:

1.  Open the **Agents** tab on GitHub.com.
2.  Select a session and open **Sharing settings** from the `...` menu.
3.  Enable sharing to give repository collaborators view-only access.

Recipients can view the session's prompts, responses, and file changes, but cannot steer or modify the session. Shared sessions are not indexed for other users' session queries.

## Session sync status

The session sync status appears in the Copilot status bar in the Chat view. It shows the current state of cloud sync:

| State                  | Description                                                                        |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Not enabled**        | Session-history sync is off. This does not delete previously synced data.          |
| **Enabled**            | Sessions are syncing to your GitHub account.                                       |
| **N sessions synced**  | Shows how many sessions have been uploaded. Select to view sessions on GitHub.com. |
| **Syncing N sessions** | Upload is in progress.                                                             |
| **Disabled by policy** | Your organization's policy prevents session sync.                                  |
| **Sync error**         | Something went wrong during the last sync. Try again later.                        |

## Privacy and data control

*   Sessions are private to you by default. Synced sessions are tied to your personal GitHub account and are accessible only to you unless you explicitly share them.
*   Before syncing, VS Code filters detected secrets by matching known patterns and secret values. This can redact tokens, API keys, and credentials, but it might not detect every secret.
*   You can turn off sync at any time by setting chat.sessionSync.enabled Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders to `false`. Existing synced sessions remain on GitHub.com until you delete them.

 Important

Avoid including secrets in prompts and tool output, and review session contents before sharing. Do not rely on secret filtering to remove every sensitive value.

## Delete synced sessions

To delete synced session data, run the **Delete Session Sync Data** command (`github.copilot.sessionSync.deleteSessions`) from the Command Palette. The command shows a picker where you select which sessions to remove. After selecting sessions, you choose the deletion scope:

*   **Delete from local and cloud**: removes session data from your machine and from GitHub.com. This action cannot be undone.
*   **Delete from cloud only**: removes session data from GitHub.com but keeps local data intact.

You can also hide or delete individual synced sessions from the **Agents** tab on GitHub.com. Hiding a session removes it from your session index so it no longer appears in query results.

 Note

The **Delete Session Sync Data** command requires session sync to be enabled. If sync is off or disabled by policy, manage previously synced sessions from the **Agents** tab on GitHub.com instead.

## Query session history with Chronicle

Use Chronicle commands or natural-language questions to search past sessions, generate standup reports, and get personalized usage tips.

### Chronicle commands

Enter these commands in the chat input:

| Command                     | Description                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `/chronicle:standup`        | Summarize recent coding sessions into a standup report, grouped by branch and repository. Covers the last 24 hours by default. |
| `/chronicle:tips`           | Analyze recent session history and suggest ways to use Copilot more effectively.                                               |
| `/chronicle:cost-tips`      | Identify opportunities to reduce token usage and Copilot cost.                                                                 |
| `/chronicle:search <query>` | Search sessions by keyword, file path, or pull request or issue reference.                                                     |
| `/chronicle:reindex`        | Rebuild the local session index and sync session data when session sync is enabled.                                            |

### Ask questions about session history

Ask free-form questions such as "What files did I edit yesterday?" or "Have I worked on anything related to the payments API?" Copilot uses semantic understanding to find relevant sessions. Use `/chronicle:search` when you want a direct content search.

### What gets tracked

The local session store records:

*   **Session metadata**: repository, branch, working directory, timestamps, and the agent or participant.
*   **Conversation turns**: user messages and assistant responses.
*   **Files touched**: file paths from tool calls.
*   **External references**: pull request numbers, issue numbers, and commit SHAs.

Data is stored in a local SQLite database. Before syncing, VS Code filters detected secrets as described in [Privacy and data control](#_privacy-and-data-control).

```

```

You can also run **Reindex Sessions** (`github.copilot.chronicle.reindex`) from the Command Palette.

Run the **Settings Sync: Configure...** command or select **Settings Sync is On** > **Settings Sync: Configure...** from the **Manage** gear menu. Choose from the following data categories:

| Data category            | Synchronized data and behavior                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Settings                 | [User settings](/docs/configure/settings), except settings with the `machine` or `machine-overridable` scope and settings that you exclude.                                                                                                      |

| UI State                 | Display language, Activity Bar and Panel entries, view layout and visibility, recently used commands, and 'Do not show again' notification choices.                                                                                              |
| Extensions               | Installed extensions and the global enablement state of built-in and installed extensions.                                                                                                                                                       |
| Profiles                 | [Profiles](/docs/configure/profiles) and their data for the selected categories. You can synchronize up to 20 profiles.                                                                                                                          |
| Prompts and Instructions | [User prompt files](/docs/agent-customization/prompt-files#_sync-user-prompt-files-across-devices) and [Local agent instructions](/docs/agents/reference/custom-instructions-reference#_user-instructions) that are stored in your user profile. |
